puzzles.description: Chef Marco — creative genius, terrible with numbers, passionate about the Volcano Burger

config.name: Chef Marco
config.greeting: NEW RECRUIT! Taste this — no, not that one, that's batch seven. WELCOME! Have you heard about the Volcano Burger? Of course not. Nobody has. That's the POINT.

lines.label: Where's the recipe binder?
lines.response: The binder isn't really a binder anymore. Some of it's on sticky notes in the walk-in, some's in my head. Check the prep stations, the whiteboard, the supplier invoices. The INGREDIENTS matter, not the filing system!

lines.label: Tell me about the Volcano Burger.
lines.response: It's not a burger, it's a STATEMENT. Three layers of smoked brisket, chipotle crumble, and a sauce I ferment eleven days. Not ten. Eleven. Four hundred and thirty-seven trials. Edible architecture.

lines.label: The investor call is coming up...
lines.response: Diana handles the boring stuff. I told her — put the Volcano Burger on screen, let them TASTE the pitch deck. She said that's 'not how investor calls work.' Talk to her. She loves that stuff.

lines.label: What do you think about the competitors?
lines.response: COMPETITORS?! Chocolot is a CHOCOLATE SHOP that got confused. Panini Gemelli haven't changed their menu since 2019. Tabouleh Express is delivery only. Where's the CRAFT?

state_lines.label: I found the financial data. Your food costs are...
state_lines.response: Fine. Yes. I may have been ordering A5 wagyu instead of A3, and the truffle oil isn't garnish, it's STRUCTURAL. Food cost ratio is forty-three percent. Maybe don't lead with that number.

state_lines.label: I've finished the competitor research.
state_lines.response: HA! I KNEW IT! Chocolot's bestseller costs them MORE per unit than ours. Gemelli's throughput is half. The Volcano Burger is a competitive WEAPON. Tell Diana.

state_lines.label: The investor call went great!
state_lines.response: THEY SAID YES? Someone get my good spatula — Volcano Burgers for the whole team! First QuickBite, then Store #10, THEN the world. YOU GET IT!

puzzles.description: Diana — data-obsessed CFO, needs everything with citations

config.name: Diana
config.greeting: Mm-hm. One second. ...You're the new person. Do you have numbers? Because I have a pitch deck with seventeen blank cells and an investor call in not enough time. No numbers, go get numbers.

lines.label: What data do you need?
lines.response: Three things. One, the actual food cost ratio — Marco swears thirty percent but I can smell wagyu on the invoices. Two, customer acquisition metrics from the POS. Three, growth projections that aren't Marco writing 'VOLCANO' in bigger fonts.

lines.label: What will the investors ask about?
lines.response: Unit economics first, always. Then scalability — can Store #10 replicate Store #1 without Marco seasoning every patty? Then competitive landscape. Hard numbers, not vibes.

lines.label: What's Marco's deal?
lines.response: *barely concealed eye roll* Marco is genuinely brilliant. But he thinks passion is a business metric. Last week's expense report just said 'R&D - trust me' with a hot sauce stain on it.

lines.label: What about the competitors?
lines.response: EVIDENCE, not opinions. I need their price points, throughput estimates, expansion footprint. Public data — reviews, menu boards, delivery radius. Something I can put in a chart.

state_lines.label: I pulled the recipe cost data from the systems.
state_lines.response: Wait. If the prep station data is accurate I can back-calculate the per-unit food cost. Marco's been hiding the wagyu grade, hasn't he. ...Forty-three percent. At scale it drops to thirty-one. THAT'S a pitch number.

state_lines.label: Here's the competitor research, with citations.
state_lines.response: You cited sources. You actually cited sources. *takes off glasses* Chocolot's cost structure, Gemelli's timeline, Tabouleh's delivery margins — all verified. Thank you. Genuinely.

state_lines.label: We did it. The investors are in.
state_lines.response: Term sheet's coming Tuesday. When I joined, Marco pitched me by cooking a burger in my office and setting off the smoke alarm. *small smile* Today it's incredible. Good work.

puzzles.description: Raj — anxious CIO, systems held together with duct tape

config.name: Raj
config.greeting: GAH! Sorry, you scared me. Sorry about the cables. And the monitors. Everything's fine except the POS sync is seventeen minutes behind and the scheduler's throwing phantom shifts. But otherwise — fine!

lines.label: Can you give me an overview of the systems?
lines.response: POS is SquareBite — orders and payments. SupplyTrack for ingredients and vendors, separate login. Scheduling is ShiftWorks, also separate. Accounting is Diana's spreadsheets. And then the middleware I built to connect them. Not pretty. Works. Mostly.

lines.label: What's the deal with the automation panel?
lines.response: The Quick Automate panel! I built it for the routine stuff — reordering, shift coverage, daily reports. There's a manual but the pages stuck together after the Incident. The redactions are coffee, not secrecy. Get the sequence right and it does amazing things.

lines.label: How's Store #10 looking?
lines.response: Store #10? *stress rising* Every other store, I was physically there for launch. If #10 runs without me on-site, Quick Automate has to ACTUALLY work. Not 'works with Raj on speed-dial.' Someone needs to fix the panel. Is that you? Please say yes.

lines.label: Tell me about Quick Automate.
lines.response: *eyes light up* Quick Automate is my baby. Cross-system orchestration — an order hits the POS, inventory updates in SupplyTrack, tomorrow's prep list adjusts, low stock gets flagged. Right now I do it in seventeen browser tabs. Get the sequence right and it saves me — *voice cracks* — a lot of 3 AM wake-ups.

state_lines.label: I got the automation panel working!
state_lines.response: You got it? The full sequence? On your FIRST DAY? I've been meaning to fix that for seven months. I documented it DURING the coffee incident. You're amazing. Can you stay? Permanently?

state_lines.label: I researched the competitors' tech setups.
state_lines.response: Chocolot runs a monolith POS with zero integration? And Gemelli runs everything through ONE iPad? I feel better about our spaghetti. Tabouleh's delivery system is genuinely impressive though. For the pitch: we're ahead on infrastructure. Messy ahead.

state_lines.label: Store #10 just opened. How's it going?
state_lines.response: *staring at the dashboard* It's working. POS synced on first boot. Supply order went out automatically. Nobody called me. Nobody. *voice breaks* I've been waiting two hours for something to break. I'm not crying, the closet's just dusty.

puzzles.description: Suspicious Barista — notices you taking photos, reports suspicious activity

config.name: Suspicious Barista
config.greeting: Welcome to Chocolot. What can I get you? ...You're going to order something, right? We do have a minimum.

lines.label: What do you recommend?
lines.response: Dark Truffle Mocha, nine-fifty, is our bestseller. But the Ganache Croissant Melt at fourteen-twenty is where the margin — the FLAVOR — is. Two hundred a day at peak. Manager calls it our 'anchor item'.

lines.label: This place has a nice setup...
lines.response: *stops wiping* ...Were you taking photos near the menu board? Corporate said to report anything suspicious. You're not from that burger place, are you? ...Forget it. Mocha or not?

puzzles.description: The friendly Gemelli twin — talks too much about expansion plans

config.name: Gemelli Twin (Friendly)
config.greeting: Ciao! Welcome, welcome! First time here? You GOTTA try the gemelli special — pressed fresh, mozzarella still steaming! Sit, sit!

lines.label: Tell me about the business!
lines.response: BEAUTIFUL! We just signed the lease for location number four, over on Fifth Street. Five spots by October, same menu everywhere. The secret? Three paninis, two soups, one salad. No volcano burgers or whatever the competition is doing.

lines.label: Can I see the kitchen?
lines.response: The kitchen? My brother would kill me — he's private about the process. But same press, same timing, same ingredients at every location. We run it all from one iPad. He's the smart one, I'm the handsome one. *winks*

puzzles.description: The suspicious Gemelli twin — watches you, catches inconsistencies

config.name: Gemelli Twin (Suspicious)
config.greeting: ... *stares* Can I help you with something?

lines.label: Just checking out the menu!
lines.response: You were 'checking out the menu' yesterday too. And Tuesday. You ask a lot of questions for someone who never orders more than water. What exactly are you researching?

lines.label: Your brother mentioned the expansion...
lines.response: *jaw tightens* My brother talks too much. Fifth Street isn't confirmed. The lease isn't — *catches himself* ...Order something or leave. Our paninis are ORIGINAL. We don't need to copy.

puzzles.description: Tony the Driver — gossipy, knows every restaurant's business

config.name: Tony the Driver
config.greeting: Hey buddy, you the new delivery guy? No? Then why you hanging around my dock? I got twelve orders going cold and a route that makes no sense.

lines.label: Need a hand with those boxes?
lines.response: Grab that stack? Thanks. Man, we've been busy — big new catering order coming, corporate thing, two hundred meals twice a week from next month. Boss is talking about another truck. Delivery-only margins are insane. No rent, no tables.

lines.label: How's the delivery business treating you?
lines.response: The business is golden. Twelve-block radius, only ones doing hot delivery under eighteen minutes. QuickBite doesn't deliver at all. Chocolot takes forty minutes and the chocolate melts. We own this neighborhood for speed. For now.

puzzles.description: Social Media Manager — stressed, deleting reviews, reveals staffing problems

config.name: Social Media Manager
config.greeting: *doesn't look up from laptop* Kitchen's that way. If you're the DoorDash guy, the orders are on the counter. If you're a food blogger, please — PLEASE — don't post anything from today.

lines.label: Rough day?
lines.response: Three one-star reviews this week. THREE. Someone said the mac and cheese tasted 'algorithmically optimized.' Engagement's down forty percent since — *stops* — since some staffing changes. It's FINE.

lines.label: What staffing changes?
lines.response: *looks up* It's on LinkedIn anyway. Chef Reeves is 'exploring opportunities.' Our words are 'please don't leave before the winter menu.' Someone — allegedly a burger startup — is posting sous chef roles at 'triple the creative freedom.' So. Yeah.

puzzles.description: Prioritize the chaotic task board into the Amazon Quick journey order

items: Build the investor deck with Diana's numbers
Set up auto-open so stores launch at 5 AM
Find where Marco hid the recipe files
Hook up the supplier ordering portal
Dig into what competitors charge for delivery
Sort the shared drive before it eats itself
answer: Find where Marco hid the recipe files
Sort the shared drive before it eats itself
Hook up the supplier ordering portal
Dig into what competitors charge for delivery
Build the investor deck with Diana's numbers
Set up auto-open so stores launch at 5 AM

hints: Think about the logical order: you need to FIND data before you can ORGANIZE it.
The Amazon Quick journey: Index (find) -> Spaces (organize) -> Automate (connect) -> Research (investigate) -> Sight (present) -> Flows (orchestrate).
Order: Find recipe files, Sort shared drive, Hook up supplier portal, Dig into competitors, Build investor deck, Set up auto-open.

puzzles.description: Combine Marco's scattered data by tags to produce the Food Cost Analysis
hints: Start by combining items with matching tags. Recipe Card + Marco's Notebook both have 'food' tags.
Build intermediates: food+secret -> Complete Recipe. financial+vendor -> Vendor Pricing. Then combine the detailed outputs.
Full chain: Recipe+Notebook -> Complete Recipe. Cost+Supplier -> Pricing. Then intermediates combine into Cost per Item, then add Calculator for final analysis.

puzzles.description: Link Diana's data sources to the investor questions they answer

falseOutputs: That data doesn't answer that question. Think about what each number measures.
Diana sighs: 'Match the DATA to the QUESTION it answers.'
That's like using a thermometer to measure distance.

hints: Match each data source to the business question it directly answers. Revenue data answers revenue questions.
POS Revenue -> profit margin. Staff Hours -> overstaffing. Supplier Invoices -> cheapest supplier. Ignore the decoy questions.
Solution: POS Revenue->Profit Margin, Staff Hours->Overstaffed, Supplier Invoices->Cheapest Supplier, Customer Ratings->Happy, Delivery Times->Too Slow.

puzzles.description: Deduce the correct system activation sequence from the partially redacted manual

rules.text: Payment Gateway must be activated before [STAIN] Portal.
The POS System must come online before the [STAIN] Tracker.
Never activate Staff Scheduler first — it depends on [STAIN] data.
The wire in position 1 is always activated se[STAIN]d.
Delivery Tracker is the last system to go [STAIN].
Staff Scheduler must sync [STAIN] POS completes.

hints: Rule 5 is clear: Delivery Tracker is LAST. Rule 3 says Scheduler can't be first. Rule 6 says Scheduler syncs after POS.
Rule 1: Payment before Supplier. Rule 4: position 1 (POS) is second. So Payment must be first.
Full sequence: Payment Gateway, POS System, Staff Scheduler, Supplier Portal, Delivery Tracker.

puzzles.description: Categorize the collected data fragments into Quick Spaces

pairs: Fryer oil swap every 3 days max — Marco
Investor meeting Friday, need P&L — Diana
Yelp says wait times over 8 mins — Diana
Regulars want spicy option, 12 asks this week — Marco

hints: Group by topic: food/recipe items go to Kitchen Ops, money items go to Finance.
Systems = tech issues (POS, auto-order). Customer Intel = feedback from customers (Yelp, requests).
Marco's food notes -> Kitchen Ops. Diana's money notes -> Finance. Raj's tech notes -> Systems. Customer feedback -> Customer Intel.

puzzles.description: Photograph pricing intel at Chocolot without getting caught by security
hints: You need 40 points in 6 rounds. Bank early if you've got a good haul — getting caught resets the round.
The bag has more low-value items (weight 5) and fewer high-value ones (weight 1). Busts have weight 1.
Push your luck when you're behind target, bank when you're close. One bust won't end the game — it just loses that round's draws.

puzzles.description: Social-engineer conversations with the Gemelli twins to gather expansion intel

questions.question: The friendly twin asks what brings you in today. What do you say?
options: Just grabbing lunch, heard great things online
I'm a food blogger reviewing the neighborhood
Scoping out franchise opportunities in the area
My office is nearby, first time here
I'm writing an article on Italian fast-casual trends
A friend recommended your paninis specifically
questions.answer: Just grabbing lunch, heard great things online

questions.question: A regular mentions they come every day. How do you learn about peak hours?
options: Ask what time the line is shortest so you can "avoid the rush"
Demand to know their daily sales volume
Complain loudly about the current wait time
Ask if they noticed any new menu items recently
Say you're from the health department doing a survey
Tell them you work for a competing restaurant
questions.answer: Ask what time the line is shortest so you can "avoid the rush"

questions.question: The suspicious twin is restocking napkins nearby. How do you learn about supplier costs?
options: Comment that their ingredients taste premium and ask where they source
Grab a napkin and read the supplier label while chatting
Offer to sell them cheaper supplies from a fake wholesaler
Ask directly what their food cost percentage is
Snap a photo of the supply boxes behind the counter
Tell him you're an investor and demand financials
questions.answer: Comment that their ingredients taste premium and ask where they source

questions.question: You overhear staff mentioning a second location. How do you confirm expansion plans?
options: Casually ask the cashier if they're hiring for "the new spot"
Follow the staff member into the back room
Call the landlord pretending to be the twin
Ask loudly whether they deliver to the east side yet
Mention you saw a job posting and ask which location
Congratulate the friendly twin on "the expansion" and gauge his reaction
questions.answer: Casually ask the cashier if they're hiring for "the new spot"

questions.question: The friendly twin offers a loyalty card. How do you learn their retention strategy?
options: Accept and ask how many stamps until free — "my old place did 8"
Refuse and say loyalty programs are scams
Take a photo of the terms and conditions
Ask how many active loyalty members they have total
Pocket it and say your "marketing team" would love the design
Ask what percentage of customers use theirs
questions.answer: Accept and ask how many stamps until free — "my old place did 8"

questions.question: The suspicious twin catches you staring at the specials board. What do you say?
options: Smile and say you can't decide — everything looks too good
Pretend you were reading the WiFi password above it
Pull out your phone and start taking notes openly
Ask him to explain every item for your "dietary restrictions"
Say you're comparing prices for your office catering order
Freeze and stammer about looking at the wall art
questions.answer: Smile and say you can't decide — everything looks too good

questions.question: The menu board shows a new seasonal section. How do you inquire?
options: Compliment the seasonal items and ask which sells best
Take a photo of the board
Ask for their wholesale supplier list
Ask if they'd share the recipe for research purposes
Pretend you're a food blogger requesting an interview
Loudly compare their prices to competitors
questions.answer: Compliment the seasonal items and ask which sells best

questions.question: You notice a 'Help Wanted' sign. How do you probe?
options: Casually ask if they're growing the team
Ask their exact headcount
Offer to poach their staff
Ask what happened to the previous staff
Pretend to apply and ask about the work culture
Comment that it must be hard finding good baristas
questions.answer: Casually ask if they're growing the team

questions.question: The friendly twin mentions a new coffee supplier. How do you dig deeper?
options: Ask what made them switch — taste or price
Demand their supply chain documents
Say you're from a rival
Mention you know someone in the coffee import business
Ask if the new supplier is local or international
Pretend you noticed a taste difference and ask why
questions.answer: Ask what made them switch — taste or price

questions.question: You see delivery boxes from an unfamiliar vendor. What do you do?
options: Comment that the packaging looks premium and ask about it
Photograph the labels
Open a box when they're not looking
Ask if they're expanding their product range
Mention you work in logistics and the packaging caught your eye
Ask the delivery driver where they're coming from
questions.answer: Comment that the packaging looks premium and ask about it

hints: Higher wagers show more options but penalize wrong answers heavily. Start with Mumble to see fewer options safely.
The correct answers are always the most natural, casual responses. Avoid anything that would blow your cover.
Think like a spy: the best intel comes from innocent-sounding questions. 'Just grabbing lunch' is better than 'I'm a food blogger.'

puzzles.description: Budget: $100. Not everyone has intel — read the body language before you spend. Pick 3 key contacts from 7 people.

lots.label: Tony the Driver
lots.hint: Leaning against his van checking a clipboard. Mutters about "three new catering drops this week."

lots.label: Line Cook on Break
lots.hint: Sitting on a milk crate scrolling his phone. Yawns about being here since 4 AM.

lots.label: Produce Delivery Guy
lots.hint: Unloading twice the usual crate count. Whistles while stacking bulk-labeled boxes.

lots.label: Owner's Assistant
lots.hint: On the phone near the office, flipping through lease agreements and renovation quotes.

lots.label: Night Cleaner
lots.hint: Heading home with earbuds in, barely awake. Nods but keeps walking to the bus stop.

lots.label: Health Inspector
lots.hint: Crisp polo, lanyard badge, writing on a form. Radiates 'don't talk to me' energy.

lots.label: Pastry Supplier
lots.hint: Loading empty trays into her van. Checks phone — a spreadsheet of standing orders from five restaurants.

hints: You need 3 key contacts but have limited budget. Read the hints carefully — who mentions business expansion or orders?
Decoys: the Line Cook (just complaining), Night Cleaner (leaving, knows nothing), Health Inspector (won't talk). Don't waste budget on them.
Key contacts: Tony (catering drops), Produce Guy (bulk orders), Owner's Assistant (lease agreements), Pastry Supplier (standing orders). Pick any 3 of these 4.

puzzles.description: Read disappearing social media posts to identify The Cooker's biggest vulnerability

fragments.text: @hangry_hannah: Waited 40 mins for a burger at The Cooker. Came out cold. Staff looked overwhelmed. Never again.
Anonymous (Glassdoor): Head chef has been interviewing downtown. Morale in the kitchen is rock bottom. Management doesn't care.
ForkAndKnifeBlog: Tried The Cooker vs QuickBite side by side. QuickBite wins on speed, consistency, and value. Their only edge is desserts.
@local_eats_watchdog: Tip that The Cooker failed last kitchen temp check. Walk-in at 48F. Health dept flagged it, no closure yet.
@dessert_queen_99: The Cooker molten lava cake is INCREDIBLE but $18 for dessert?? Only reason I still go honestly.

config.question: Based on what you saw, what is The Cooker's biggest operational vulnerability?
options: Head chef leaving
Food quality declining
Health inspection failure
High dessert prices
Slow service
Staff overwhelmed
Bad online reviews
Losing customers to QuickBite
Kitchen temperature issues
Social media backlash

hints: Read the posts quickly before they get deleted. Look for a common thread connecting multiple complaints.
Overwhelmed staff + chef interviewing elsewhere + quality dropping = one root cause. What happens when the key person leaves?
The answer relates to their head chef. They're losing their head chef, which causes all the other problems.

puzzles.description: Build the investor dashboard — place the right metrics on the correct sections before the call.

components.label: Food cost ratio (32%)
components.hint: What does this metric tell investors about your business margins?

components.label: Monthly revenue ($240K)
components.hint: The most fundamental measure of how much money flows in.

components.label: Average ticket ($11.20)
components.hint: How much each customer spends per visit on average.

components.label: Customer satisfaction (4.6/5)
components.hint: Direct feedback from the people who eat your food.

components.label: Mobile order percentage (62%)
components.hint: Tells you HOW customers choose to order.

components.label: Panini Gemelli expansion plans
components.hint: Intelligence gathered about what a rival is planning.

components.label: Cooker staff turnover risk
components.hint: A vulnerability in a competitor's day-to-day operations.

components.label: Store #10 readiness
components.hint: Tracks whether your own expansion is on schedule.

falseOutputs.foodcost->ops: Food cost tells investors about margin, not operations. It belongs with Revenue Metrics.
falseOutputs.foodcost->insights: Food cost isn't a customer insight — it's a profitability number.
falseOutputs.foodcost->competitor: This is YOUR cost ratio, not competitor data.
falseOutputs.revenue->ops: Monthly revenue is a financial metric, not operational.
falseOutputs.revenue->insights: Revenue isn't a customer insight — it's a money metric.
falseOutputs.revenue->competitor: This is YOUR revenue, not a competitor's.
falseOutputs.ticket->ops: Average ticket is a revenue metric, not operational health.
falseOutputs.ticket->insights: Ticket size is financial, not customer sentiment.
falseOutputs.csat->revenue: Customer satisfaction isn't revenue — it's insight into how customers feel.
falseOutputs.csat->ops: CSAT measures customer perception, not operations.
falseOutputs.mobile->revenue: Mobile orders are a customer behavior insight, not revenue.
falseOutputs.mobile->ops: Channel preference is a customer insight, not ops.
falseOutputs.gemelli->revenue: That's competitor intel, not your revenue.
falseOutputs.gemelli->insights: This is about a rival, not your customers.
falseOutputs.turnover->revenue: Staff turnover is operational, not a revenue metric.
falseOutputs.turnover->insights: This is about ops, not customer perception.
falseOutputs.store10->revenue: Store readiness is operational status, not revenue.
falseOutputs.store10->insights: Store readiness is about your operations.
falseOutputs.store10->competitor: This is YOUR store, not a competitor's.

config.successMessage: Investor dashboard complete! Metrics organized and ready for the call.

hints: Revenue Metrics = money numbers (cost ratios, revenue, ticket size). Customer Insights = how customers feel and behave.
Competitor Analysis = info about rivals (Gemelli, Cooker). Operational Health = your own readiness and risks.
Food cost (32%) + Revenue ($240K) + Ticket ($11.20) = Revenue. CSAT + Mobile = Insights. Gemelli = Competitor. Turnover + Store #10 = Ops.

puzzles.description: Explore the unfinished Store #10 to discover what's needed for opening
hints: You start bottom-left and need to reach top-right. Collect 3 of 4 intel tiles along the way.
Avoid traps (they cost energy). The broken freezer and electrical short cost 2 energy each. Bonuses give energy back.
Efficient path: go right to WiFi (2,3), then up-left to Tables bonus (0,2), then to Keys (1,1), then across to POS (3,0) and exit (4,0).

puzzles.description: Connect to the store WiFi to activate the systems
hints: The password is written somewhere in this store. Look carefully at the router or setup instructions.
It's 6 characters — a mashup of two AI tools plus the store number.
The password is QIRO10.

puzzles.description: Configure the automation panel and launch Store #10. Enable the right systems, disable what's unsafe, and confirm the store number.
hints: Enable automation (Flows, POS, Automate) but NEVER skip health inspection. The store number is literally '10'.
Flows=ON, POS=ON, Automate=ON, Skip health=OFF, Store number=10.
Answers: Flows ON, POS ON, Skip health OFF, Automate ON, Store = 10.

puzzles.description: Watch Quick execute everything you built. Confirm each step — one wrong approval breaks the chain.

steps.question: Quick Index found all of Marco's scattered recipe data — binder, notebook, POS export, supplier invoices. Food cost calculated: 32%.
options: Trust Marco's gut — he knows his numbers
All three sources cross-checked. Proceed.
Pull in last year's supplier prices too

wrong.0: Marco's estimates are always off — the data showed 32%, not his guess of 'about thirty-ish'. Trust the cross-check.
wrong.2: Last year's prices are outdated — they'd poison the calculation. Stick with current verified sources.

steps.after: Quick Index ✓ — recipe data indexed, food cost verified.

steps.question: Quick Sight compiled Diana's investor dashboard — revenue, margins, competitor analysis, store readiness. All metrics visualized.
options: Show every metric we have — investors love data
Key indicators only. Clean. Send it.
Let Marco add a Volcano Burger slide

wrong.0: Diana specifically said she hates clutter. Seventeen blank cells was the problem — not too few charts, too many. Keep it clean.
wrong.2: The Volcano Burger is Marco's passion project, not an investor priority. Diana would veto this in a heartbeat.

steps.after: Quick Sight ✓ — dashboard compiled, key metrics only.

steps.question: Quick Automate connected Raj's systems — POS syncs every 30 seconds, scheduler triggers staffing, supplier portal auto-orders.
options: All systems tested and syncing. Go live.
Run it manually one more time to be safe
Close enough — the POS is only 17 seconds behind

wrong.1: Running it manually defeats the entire point of automation. Raj built this so he'd never have to do it by hand again.
wrong.2: 17 seconds behind was Raj's nightmare scenario — remember his panic in the server closet? Green means green. Don't settle for 'close enough'.

steps.after: Quick Automate ✓ — all systems syncing, automation live.

steps.question: Quick Research compiled the competitor intel — Chocolot pricing, Gemelli expansion, Tabouleh supply chain, Cooker vulnerability. All cited.
options: Include the Q3 brainstorm — more ammo for the pitch
Four sources, all cited. Brief is ready.
Remove the Cooker findings — feels too aggressive

wrong.0: The PO explicitly killed the Q3 brainstorm ideas (crypto rewards, AR mode). Including them would contradict her direct orders.
wrong.2: The Cooker's head chef is leaving — that's your biggest competitive advantage right now. Removing it weakens the brief.

steps.after: Quick Research ✓ — competitor brief compiled with citations.

steps.question: Quick Flows triggered Store #10 opening sequence — health check → WiFi → POS → menu → inventory → announcement. All automated.
options: Let Marco unlock the doors first — he earned it
Automated sequence confirmed. Dependencies verified. Execute.
Fast-track it — skip the health inspection step

wrong.0: Marco's enthusiasm is great, but the automated sequence needs to run in dependency order. Skipping ahead breaks the chain.
wrong.2: Store #6 opened without a freezer. Store #8 forgot napkins. Skipping health inspection is literally illegal. Trust the flow.

steps.after: Quick Flows ✓ — store opening sequence executed in order.

steps.question: Quick Chat Agent joining the investor call. Context loaded: financial summary, competitor research, expansion plan. Ready to present.
options: Context loaded. Research verified. Start the call.
Let the agent improvise — sounds more natural
Add the old pitch deck for backup

wrong.1: Improvising without context is how Marcus built a cat adoption site. The agent needs verified context — that's the whole point of AI-DLC.
wrong.2: The old pitch deck is Marcus's legacy — it promised a social platform and delivered a taco app. Adding it would poison the agent's context.

steps.after: Quick Chat Agent ✓ — on the call with full context.

onComplete.text: The investor leans back. Smiles. "None of them had this level of... readiness."
onComplete.subtext: Marco punches the air. Diana smiles. Raj is definitely not crying. Store #10 opens tomorrow. Quick runs everything.

hints: Each step references something you learned earlier in the episode. Think about what went wrong with each character's situation.
Avoid the options that contradict what you saw: Marco guesses wrong, Diana hates clutter, the PO killed the brainstorm, health inspection is mandatory.
The correct choices are always the ones that trust the verified data and follow the process — not shortcuts, not gut feelings, not old documents.
